title: Om jai jagadish hare
carry: victory to the lord of the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, arti at home: a small flame, circled clockwise. Your line was light, circled. What did you notice yourself circling back to? Day one hundred and twenty.

A housewarming. The living room is packed, shoes piled by the door. Someone lights the lamp, someone rings a bell, and an aunt starts a tune. By the second line the room has joined in. Grandparents sing it loudly. Teenagers half-sing it. You could hear the same tune at a Diwali party, or on a Sunday evening at a temple in Houston or Leicester or Nairobi. Yesterday you circled the flame. Today: the song that often goes with it.
screen: `A PACKED ROOM, ONE TUNE.` → `LIVING ROOMS AND TEMPLES.` → `TODAY: THE ARTI SONG.`

segments.voice: The song is Om jai jagadish hare. It isn't ancient. It's usually credited to Shardha Ram Phillauri, a Punjabi writer of the eighteen-hundreds, and it's in Hindi, not Sanskrit. Some say that's part of why it spread: anyone could understand it. Here's the first line, the one everybody knows: Om jai jagadish hare, swami jai jagadish hare. Let's open it word by word. Om, the first sound, your word from day two. Jai, victory, or glory, the word people shout at festivals. Jagadish is two words joined: jagat, the world, the moving universe, and ish, lord. The lord of the world. And hare calls on Hari, a name of Vishnu that tradition explains as the one who takes away. Swami means master, lord. So: Om, victory to you, lord of the world, O Hari. Victory, master, to the lord of the world. Then the verse goes on to say why: the troubles of your devotees, of those who serve you, you take away in a moment. That's the whole song in small. It isn't a request list. It starts with praise, jai, and only then remembers that people are hurting and trusts that help comes quickly. The song is addressed to Vishnu, but it's often sung at the end of other pujas too, to whatever form is on the shelf. And it's sung while the flame circles: the tune and the light move together.
screen: `NOT ANCIENT, AND IN HINDI.` · `JAI — VICTORY, GLORY.` · `JAGAT + ISH: LORD OF THE WORLD.` · `PRAISE FIRST, THEN THE TROUBLES.`

segments.voice: Let's try it, slowly, even if singing isn't your thing. You can speak it, or just listen inside. Om jai jagadish hare. Swami jai jagadish hare. Once more, a little slower, and if you'd like, hold your flame or your open hand and let it circle with the tune. Om jai jagadish hare. Swami jai jagadish hare. Then let the sound stop and sit in what's left of it. If you don't pray, you can simply listen to the words and the tune. The bell holds the time.
Om jai jagadish hare. The arti song: Om, victory to you, lord of the world, O Hari. Today's word.
Your line: victory to the lord of the world. Today, before you ask for anything, start with one line of thanks or praise, and notice how the asking changes. Day one hundred and twenty.

howItsDone: In many Hindu homes and temples, especially in North India and the diaspora, Om jai jagadish hare is sung while the arti lamp is circled at the end of puja, with a bell ringing and everyone joining in.
